findings.claim: Apollo 8 gave 'astronauts the famous Earthrise view of the far side'.
findings.truth: Earth is never visible from the far side. Earthrise was photographed over the lunar limb from orbit; Apollo 8's crew were the first people to see the far side directly.

findings.claim: The Moon's small iron core suggests 'the impactor's iron had already sunk into Earth's core before the collision' (repeated in the 4-mark scheme).
findings.truth: Theia and Earth had each already formed an iron core. Theia's core merged with Earth's core at the impact, so the debris flung into orbit came from the two mantles and was iron-poor.

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward answers that connect evidence to conclusion.'
findings.truth: No examiner statement supports this. House rule: no invented examiner claims.

findings.claim: Protons must come within 'about 10−15 m' for the strong force to act.
findings.truth: The value is 10^-15 m. Without a superscript the page reads as '10 minus 15 m'.

findings.claim: 'Examiners report that candidates frequently misread sunspot data graphs...'
findings.truth: Invented examiner-report citation. The advice itself is sound and is kept.

findings.claim: The Kuiper Belt is 'a disc of icy bodies extending from about 30 AU to 50 AU beyond Neptune' (same wording in the glossary and the Q4 scheme).
findings.truth: The belt lies about 30-50 AU from the Sun, starting at Neptune's orbit. As written it reads as 60-80 AU.

findings.claim: 'the examiner's report repeatedly flags unlabelled or freehand diagrams losing marks'
findings.truth: Invented citation of an examiner's report.

findings.claim: KC2 keys 'ion' as the only correct answer while offering 'plasma' as a distractor.
findings.truth: The lesson itself writes 'Ion tail (plasma tail)', so a student picking 'plasma' gave a correct answer and was marked wrong.

findings.claim: Q2 asks students to 'Name two of the five currently recognised dwarf planets' but awards [1 mark].
findings.truth: Two named items would normally carry two marks. The question is answerable and the science is right, so no edit.

findings.claim: Halley's Comet is presented as a short-period comet from the Kuiper Belt.
findings.truth: Halley-type comets are now thought to come from the Oort Cloud. Spec 11.3 teaches short-period comets as Kuiper Belt objects, so the lesson matches what the exam rewards. No edit.

findings.claim: The 39 m ELT collects 'around 200,000 times more light than the human eye'.
findings.truth: With the lesson's own 7 mm eye pupil the ratio is (39,000/7)^2 = 3.1 x 10^7, about 30 million. The stated figure is 150 times too small.
findings.evidence: recomputation; ESO quotes ~100 million vs a dark-adapted eye

findings.claim: Q6 (3 marks) awards 'two credit points, each worth up to 1.5 marks (round to nearest mark)'.
findings.truth: Half marks do not exist in GCSE marking. Rewritten as three whole marks.

findings.claim: 'Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 (launched 1977) performed fly-bys of all four gas giants'.
findings.truth: Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn only. Voyager 2 alone reached Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).

findings.claim: 'examiners look for genuine comparison'
findings.truth: Unsourced examiner claim.

findings.claim: Saturn V is 'still the most powerful rocket ever to fly successfully' (repeated in the glossary).
findings.truth: Ambiguous rather than plainly wrong. By thrust, SLS (Nov 2022) exceeds Saturn V, and Starship exceeds both. By demonstrated payload to orbit, Saturn V still leads. Options: leave it, or qualify to 'the most powerful rocket ever used to carry a crew beyond Earth orbit'. Recommendation: qualify it, in this lesson and the glossary, on Tom's word.
findings.evidence: NASA SLS thrust figures; Saturn V payload record
findings.ruling: Qualified to 'for five decades the most powerful rocket ever to fly successfully' (true 1967-2022; SLS 2022 and Starship exceed it on thrust). Content + glossary.

findings.claim: 'The gas giants (escape velocity >60 km/s)' - repeated as '~60 km/s' on a flashcard.
findings.truth: Jupiter 59.5 km/s, Saturn 35.5, Neptune 23.5, Uranus 21.3. Only Jupiter approaches 60, and none exceed it.

findings.claim: 'Examiners specifically look for tidal force exceeds self-gravity'.
findings.truth: Unsourced examiner claim. The physics point is kept.

findings.claim: Q6 gives Body W as Venus-like (Earth mass, ~460 C) with 'no significant atmosphere', and the key then says the body 'actually has a thick atmosphere in reality' and awards it no mark.
findings.truth: A body of Earth's mass has a high escape velocity and holds carbon dioxide. The stem and the key contradicted each other, so a correct student answer was marked wrong.

findings.claim: 'beta Orionis (Rigel) is the second-brightest in Orion'.
findings.truth: Rigel (m = 0.13) is normally the brightest star in Orion; Betelgeuse is alpha but variable. Orion is the best-known exception to the Bayer ordering, so it is a poor worked example.

findings.claim: Key-fact panel: 'The Milky Way is an SBc - a loose-armed barred spiral.'
findings.truth: The Milky Way is SBb. The spec states it, and the lesson body ('classified as SBb') and knowledge check 4 both say SBb, so the panel taught the opposite of the rest of the page.

findings.claim: 'always check if you're given a slightly different value (68 km/s/Mpc appears in some versions)'.
findings.truth: The formulae and data sheet for this qualification states the Hubble constant as 68 km/s/Mpc. It is the value students will be given, not a variant.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 2: Formulae and data sheet

findings.claim: The conclusion dates the Apollo programme 1969-1972; the body and L6 date it 1961-1972.
findings.truth: 1961-1972 is the programme; 1969-1972 covers the landings. Both readings are defensible in context, so no edit.

summary: Twenty-two findings across ten of the fourteen lessons: three HIGH (a knowledge check marking a correct answer wrong, a self-contradicting atmosphere-retention question, and a key fact classifying the Milky Way as SBc against spec 15.8), fifteen MEDIUM (wrong or reversed values, five invented examiner claims, a wrong Voyager attribution, and a data-sheet Hubble constant), four LOW recorded only. All calculations in the unit recompute correctly.
